title: Multiple Comparisons, FWER and Forking Paths
summary: Experiment 1 runs a family of real two-sample t-tests in which every null is true, draws one square per test with the significant ones crossed, and sets the counted family-wise error rate beside 1 minus (1 minus alpha) to the power k; a Bonferroni option then shows the false-positive rate collapse and, in the same readout, the detection rate for the real effects collapsing with it. Experiment 2 generates ninety fictional students with no group difference on anything and offers four outcomes, three exclusion rules, three subgroups and two covariate decisions - seventy-two complete, defensible analyses of the same empty data - and lets the learner search until something reaches p below .05, then reveals how many other paths would have done the same. A closing challenge separates planned multiplicity, exploratory analysis, undisclosed selective reporting and confirmatory inference.
learningObjectives: Compute a family-wise error rate and say which family of tests it belongs to.
Describe what a Bonferroni correction buys and what it costs, in the same breath.
Explain how ordinary analytic flexibility inflates false positives without anyone intending to cheat.
Explain why a reported p-value assumes it was the only analysis run.
Distinguish planned multiplicity, exploratory analysis, undisclosed selective reporting and confirmatory inference.
interactionTypes: correction with its cost shown alongside
guided search through an analysis space
reveal of every path not taken
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every test and every fictional student is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups, a number input and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the sliders announce meanings in words such as 'every null in the family is true'. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - a four-row breakdown of the most recent experiment by whether each test had anything to find, and a six-row description of the analysis currently selected together with the search so far - and disclosures hold the theory-beside-simulation table and the distribution of all 72 paths. A significant test is marked with a cross as well as a fill, a test with a real effect to find is drawn with a heavier outline, the currently selected path is ringed, and the goal checklist writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' in words, so nothing is carried by colour. Pinned primary results measure 477px and 463px tall at 1366x768. Every run, correction change and path announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to each experiment's heading as it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Why flexibility inflates false positives without anyone cheating, and what a correction costs
simulationNotes: Experiment 1 runs k genuine two-sample t-tests on 40 per group rather than drawing p-values from a uniform, so the grid on screen is an actual analysis; a chosen number of the tests carry a real effect of d = 0.60 and the rest have nothing to find. At k = 20 and alpha .05 the predicted family-wise rate is 64.2 per cent and a thousand simulated experiments give 63.0 per cent, with 1.00 predicted false positives per experiment against 0.98 counted. With five real effects among the twenty and no correction, 53.2 per cent of experiments produce at least one false positive and 75.6 per cent of the real effects are detected; switching Bonferroni on takes the threshold to .0025, the family-wise rate to 3.9 per cent counted against 4.9 predicted, and the detection rate down to 33.9 per cent - the trade is deliberately shown in one readout. Experiment 2 generates ninety fictional students, half in each group, with four correlated outcomes, a baseline test, a response-speed measure and a cohort label, and with no group difference on anything; each of the 72 paths filters the rows by exclusion rule and subgroup, optionally residualises the outcome on the baseline score, and runs a pooled two-sample t-test, so the paths are heavily correlated exactly as a real analyst's would be and no simple correction applies. On the default dataset five of the 72 reach p below .05 and the smallest is p = .026, and every one of those is a false positive by construction. The tool never presents the search as a technique: the goal banner and the feedback both say that it is a demonstration of what searching does to the meaning of the resulting p-value, and that every choice offered is one a careful researcher might make in good faith. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study, participant or dataset is involved.
